"Cussed" means stubbornly difficult, contrary, and obstinate in a way that frustrates or annoys other people. A cussed person refuses to cooperate, refuses to budge from their position, and often seems to enjoy being troublesome. It is an informal, colloquial word, used especially in American English, and it carries a strong flavor of exasperation — the speaker is not just describing someone; they are expressing frustration about them.

Stubbornness alone does not make someone cussed. A cussed person has a particular flavor of stubbornness — one that feels almost willful and unreasonable, as if they are being difficult on purpose, or as if difficult behavior is simply baked into their very nature. It is not just that they won't cooperate; it is that no amount of reasoning, pleading, or pressure will move them even a little. There is something almost defiant about it.

Think of it this way: a regular stubborn person might dig their heels in on something important to them. A cussed person digs their heels in on everything, almost as a personality trait, sometimes for no good reason at all — and they do not seem sorry about it.

This is why the word carries a tone of helpless irritation from the person using it. When someone calls another person cussed, they are essentially saying: "I've tried, and there is simply no getting through to this person."

1. Describing a person's character

This is the most common use. A cussed person is one who is ornery, contrary, and impossible to deal with. They resist change. They resist advice. They resist being told what to do. They may be grumpy, ill-tempered, or simply contrary by nature.

"He's the most cussed old man in the village — you can't reason with him about anything."

"She had a cussed streak in her that made her refuse help even when she desperately needed it."

Notice here that the word doesn't just mean "stubborn." It suggests the stubbornness is a deep, almost permanent part of who they are — and that it makes life harder for everyone around them.

2. Describing a thing that seems to resist and frustrate you

People also use "cussed" humorously or expressively to describe an object or a situation that seems almost deliberately uncooperative — as if it has a will of its own and has decided to be difficult.

"That cussed car broke down again right when I needed it most."

"No matter what I did, the cussed lid wouldn't come off the jar."

Here, the speaker is not seriously claiming the car or the lid is stubborn. They are venting frustration in a colorful way, as if the object has a personality and has chosen to be infuriating.
The Emotional Tone of the Word

This is important to understand, because the tone is part of the meaning.

"Cussed" is not a neutral, clinical word. It is a word you use when you are fed up. It is the word someone reaches for after they've tried everything and gotten nowhere. There is a kind of exasperated resignation in it — like throwing your hands up and saying, "That's just the way this person (or thing) is."

At the same time, the word is not extremely harsh or cruel. It does not carry deep hatred. It is more like the grumbling of someone who is worn down and frustrated. In fact, it can sometimes even be used with a grain of grudging affection — the way a person might describe an old friend or family member who drives them crazy but whom they love anyway.

"My grandfather was a cussed, impossible old man — and we adored him."
How Cussed Differs from Similar Words

There are several words that overlap with "cussed," but each has a slightly different angle.

Stubborn is the closest equivalent, but it is much more neutral. Stubborn simply means unwilling to change. Cussed adds the suggestion that the stubbornness is unreasonable, is a core part of someone's nature, and is causing frustration to others.

Ornery is very similar to cussed and is often used in the same contexts. Both are informal American English words. Ornery leans a bit more toward bad-tempered and cranky, while cussed leans slightly more toward sheer, defiant willfulness. In practice, the two words are nearly interchangeable and many speakers use them the same way.

Obstinate and pigheaded also mean stubbornly refusing to change one's mind, but they are more straightforwardly descriptive. Cussed feels more emotionally charged — it has that built-in frustration and that sense of a trait being deep and incurable.
Register: When and Where People Use This Word

"Cussed" is an informal, colloquial word. You would not find it in a formal essay, a legal document, or a scientific paper. It belongs to spoken language and casual writing — storytelling, regional speech, dialogue in fiction, and moments of colorful expression.

It has a distinctly folksy, rustic quality to it, and you will encounter it frequently in American literature and speech, particularly in older writing or writing that depicts rural or traditional communities. When a character in a novel uses the word "cussed," you immediately get a sense of their plain-spoken, no-nonsense personality.

"Cussed," as an adjective, means stubbornly, willfully, and almost defiantly difficult — whether applied to a person whose nature makes them impossible to reason with, or to a thing that seems to resist and frustrate you at every turn. The word is not just a description; it is an expression of exasperation. It is informal, it is colorful, and it tells you not just what something is like, but how it makes you feel to deal with it.
